Rare 1964 Chevy Corvette Convertible L75 327/300 Rocks Gorgeous Saddle Tan, Has an Ace up Its Sleeve
31 photos
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales
This 1964 Chevrolet Corvette Convertible looks better than it did the day it rolled off the production line 62 years ago. It rocks the Saddle Tan gold finish over a matching Saddle Tan interior and a V8 engine, which makes it extremely rare.
General Motors produced a total of 22,229 Corvettes for the 1964 model year. Of them, 13,925 were convertibles, making up 62.6% of the total production run that year. And wait, the selection narrows even further.
Only 1,765 units across all engine types and body styles rolled off the production line in the rarest factory color offered for the 1964 lineup, Saddle Tan. Only 520 of them were convertibles. And this car right here is one of them.
Often described as gold, the official factory name for this iconic metallic shade was Saddle. Tan, Paint Code 932. It stands out as one of the most distinctive, period-correct color combinations of the C2 generation, highlighting the clean lines of the 1964 redesign.
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales This model year saw the removal of the previous year's faux hood vents and the addition of functional body ventilation on the driver's side, which meant a smoother overall silhouette. This car comes with NCRS Top Flight, which is the highest and most prestigious judging award presented by the National Corvette Restorers Society.
It is essentially the gold standard for Corvette restoration. To earn a Top Flight award, a Chevy Corvette must undergo a rigorous, highly detailed raw-point inspection process by a panel of NCRS master judges. The presence of the "NCRS" letters explain the asking price.
This car is pushed forward by the 327-cubic-inch V8 , with a single four-barrel carburetor. The V8 produces 300 horsepower (304 metric horsepower) and 360 pound-feet (488 Newton meters) of torque. A Muncie four-speed manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels in pure Corvette fashion, which makes it a pure driver’s car.
At the time, General Motors also offered the two-speed Powerglide automatic transmission. While the manual car was good for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.0 seconds and a top speed of 129 mph (208 kph), the automatic did 0 to 60 in 6.8 seconds and hit a top speed of 127 mph (204 kph).
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales Finding a 1964 Convertible in Saddle Tan over a matching tan interior is rare nowadays. Well-preserved, numbers-matching examples can go as far as $90,320, as indicated by classic.com. However, Vanguard Motors has listed this example for $169,900, which is nearly double the best-maintained cars out there. The price includes two convertible tops in body-matching color.
Back in 1964, the starting price for a C2 Chevy Corvette was exactly $4,037. The L75 327-cubic-inch V8 with 300 horsepower was a $53 option at the time. Meanwhile, the Saddle Tan Metallic paint was offered at no extra cost, since it was a standard factory choice that year.
